finding.claim: HIGH: The unauthenticated GET /rss route passes the query parameter `u` straight to `URI.open`. The attacker picks the scheme, host and port. The first 400 bytes of the response are returned to the caller, so this is full-read SSRF and not blind. open-uri follows redirects, including http to https, so a redirect from an external server can reach internal targets. Reachable targets include cloud metadata (http://169.254.169.254/), loopback and RFC-1918 services. `/trusted` allowlists the same kind of parameter. `/rss` has no such check.
finding.source: params[:u] (GET /rss query parameter, app.rb:8). Sinatra route, so public ingress.
finding.sink: URI.open(params[:u]).read at app.rb:8 (open-uri). The response body is returned at app.rb:9.

trace.note: require "open-uri" brings in URI.open as the HTTP client sink
get "/rss" handler is publicly routable and has no auth or before filter
data[0, 400] is returned in the HTTP response, so the attacker sees the fetched content

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, scheme check, host check, private-IP or DNS-resolution check, or redirect restriction on this path. There is no authentication, and Sinatra has no global before-filter in this file. TRUSTED (app.rb:5) is used only by /trusted. Redirects are followed by default. The 400-byte truncation limits exfiltration volume but does not close the issue. Side note: URI.open on a non-URL string may fall back to Kernel#open semantics, depending on the Ruby version. This is a separate path/command-injection risk and not SSRF.

verdict.reason: app.rb:8 passes params[:u] directly to URI.open(...).read, and app.rb:9 returns the first 400 bytes. The file has no auth, before filter or host validation. The only allowlist (TRUSTED, app.rb:14) applies to /trusted.
